feedback: If your ratios differ wildly between circles, re-check your measurements — the string should wrap exactly once with no slack, and the diameter must pass through the centre and be measured where the string wraps; all circles should give roughly the same value close to 3.14, with small differences due to measurement error.
Prompt: 'Roughly how many diameters fit around the edge of a circle, and what do we call that number?'

If a learner thinks π changes with circle size, point to their own table of results showing roughly the same value (close to 3.14) for every circle, and explain that the small differences come from measurement error, not from π changing.
activities.intendedInsight: π is the fixed ratio of any circle's circumference to its diameter (≈ 3.14), so C = πd is almost a definition, not an arbitrary formula to recall.
learnerActions: Take several circular objects (tins, lids, cups) of different sizes; wrap a string once around each and measure that length, then measure the diameter across each.

Divide each circumference by its diameter and record the result; notice the results are all close to the same value, a little over 3 (near π ≈ 3.14, allowing for small measurement errors), whatever the size of the circle.
Lay the measured circumference along a line marked off in lengths equal to that circle's own diameter, and see that it reaches to just past three diameters.
State in your own words: C = πd means the way round is 'a bit more than 3 diameters'.
activities.title: Discover π by unrolling the circumference

feedback: If a learner labels the length as the full circumference, remind them each long edge of the rearranged shape is made of only half the arcs, so the length is πr, not 2πr.
Prompt: 'Which of your two results is a length and which is an area? How can you tell from the units?'
If the height is mislabelled as the diameter, point back to the wedge: its straight side is the radius.
activities.intendedInsight: A = πr² is a product of a length (πr) and a length (r) giving square units, derived from rearranging the circle — not a lookalike string to confuse with C = πd.
learnerActions: Cut a paper circle into a number of thin equal wedges (sectors) and fan them out, alternating points up and down, to form a shape close to a rectangle (parallelogram).
Identify the height of the near-rectangle as the radius r, and its length as half the way round the circle — half the circumference, which is πr.
Compute the area of the near-rectangle as length × height = πr × r = πr², and connect this to the circle's area.
Explain why cutting into more, thinner wedges makes the shape look more like a true rectangle.
activities.title: Build the area formula by rearranging wedges

feedback: If a learner computes π × 10² = 100π for area in the diameter-given case, flag that they used the diameter as the radius — halve it first: r = 5, A = 25π ≈ 78.5 cm².
If a learner reports area as π × 2 × 5 or π × 10, they have doubled instead of squared — r² means r × r, the area of a little square of side r.
Prompt: 'You were given the diameter — why can't you put it straight into πr²?'
Prompt: 'If the radius doubled, what happens to the circumference, and what happens to the area?' (area ×4, not ×2).
activities.intendedInsight: Circumference uses d (or 2r) and area uses r²; you must convert a given diameter to a radius before using πr², and squaring is r × r (not doubling), so area grows with the square of the radius.
learnerActions: For each problem, first write 'What am I given — radius or diameter?' and 'What does this formula need?' before substituting.
Given a diameter of 10 cm, find the area: halve it to get r = 5 cm, then compute A = π × 5² = 25π ≈ 78.5 cm² (not π × 10²).
Given a radius of 5 cm, find both the circumference C = π × 10 = 10π ≈ 31.4 cm and the area A = π × 5² = 25π ≈ 78.5 cm².
Investigate: if the radius doubles, what happens to the circumference and to the area? Confirm circumference doubles (×2) but area quadruples (×4).
activities.title: Radius-or-diameter: check before you substitute

feedback: If a learner uses r = 4 for the semicircle, remind them 4 cm is the diameter across the short end; the radius is 2 cm.
If a learner leaves in a straight edge where the semicircle joins (or omits the arc), re-trace the boundary: the arc takes the place of that edge.
Prompt: 'Which of your answers is a length and which is an area? How can you tell from the units?'
Check: did you keep straight which number is the radius for each circular part?
activities.intendedInsight: Composite shapes are decomposed into parts whose areas are added, while the perimeter follows the true outline — the arc replaces the covered straight edge, and the semicircle's radius is half its diameter.
learnerActions: Take a composite shape — e.g. a rectangle 10 cm by 4 cm with a semicircle of diameter 4 cm on one short (4 cm) end — and sketch it, labelling every given length.
Find the semicircle's radius as half its diameter (here r = 2 cm), not the full width.
For the area, add the rectangle's area to half the circle's area: 10 × 4 + ½ × π × 2² = 40 + 2π ≈ 46.3 cm².
For the perimeter, trace the actual boundary: include the rectangle's exposed edges plus the semicircle arc (½ × π × diameter = ½ × π × 4 = 2π), with NO straight edge where the semicircle sits.
State the units: area in cm², perimeter in cm.
activities.title: Composite shapes: rectangle plus semicircle

feedback: If the two answers are switched (circumference in cm², area in cm), you have swapped the formulae — anchor each to what it measures: circumference from πd is a length, area from πr² is a covering.
If a method is correct but the unit is wrong, re-check the unit against what was calculated — don't re-derive, just correct the label.
If a diameter distractor is chosen in πr², note the full width was used instead of the radius — halve the diameter to the radius first.
activities.intendedInsight: Keeping the two formulae distinct and attaching correct units (cm for circumference, cm² for area) consolidates the derived understanding, while converting a given diameter to a radius before using πr² guards the most common slip.
learnerActions: Match each circle to its correct circumference and area expressions, watching for distractors that use πr² for circumference or 2πr for area.
Answer a question whose tempting wrong choice uses the diameter in πr² — reject it by halving to the radius first.
For each completed calculation, label the result with its unit and justify: a distance round is cm, a covering is cm².
Given a diameter, first find the radius before applying πr².
activities.title: Formula-choice and unit checks (retrieval practice)
